sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Pinal County?
sections.html:
Record it with the Pinal County Recorder's Office, which has its main office in Florence and four more offices around the county. Under A.R.S. 11-468, as the county quotes it, an instrument is recorded in Pinal County when the property is located there. The office keeps public records for personal and business use and also runs voter registration and early voting.

Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132. Two limits on the staff are worth knowing before you call. The office does not provide notary services, and it is prohibited from giving legal advice, helping complete documents or suggesting which type of document to use. Your title company, escrow officer or attorney handles those questions.

Arizona law also requires a deed to be signed by the grantor and acknowledged before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). Get the notary done before the deed arrives at the counter.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Pinal County?
sections.html:
The fee is $30 per document, or $15 when the United States, the state or a political subdivision requests the recording. The county's Recording Fee Schedule is dated July 1, 2019 and follows the amendment to A.R.S. 11-475(A). It says the new fee already covers the affidavit of property value, additional indexing and the document and storage fee surcharge, and each recording fee includes $1 for postage to return the document by mail.

  • Subdivision plats or maps (24 by 36 inches): $24, with $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Survey and other maps (18 by 24 inches): $24, with $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Plats and survey maps recorded at a government agency's request: $14 for the first sheet and $10 for each additional sheet.
  • Copies of recorded documents: $1 per page, with mail requests including return postage, plus $3 per document for certification.

The schedule shows flat per-document amounts and no charge that varies with the price of the house. If you want to confirm that nothing else applies to your sale, ask the title company handling the closing.

sections.h2: How do you submit a document to the Pinal County Recorder?
sections.html:
You can record in person at any of the five offices, by mail, or electronically through a Pinal County trusted e-recording partner. For mail, send the original document with a check or money order for the amount on the fee schedule. For e-recording, contact an office for the list of partners. The county's online document search covers records from May 23, 1980 to the current end date, and downloaded images carry an unofficial copy watermark.

Photo ID is required for in-person recording under A.R.S. 11-472, with exceptions for documents submitted by an escrow office, a title insurer or agent, a bank or credit union, an active State Bar of Arizona member, or a government entity. Most sellers who close through escrow skip this because the escrow office submits the deed.

The Recorder describes what happens after you submit a compliant document in order.

  • If the form is complete and the fees are paid, the office makes it a permanent public record.
  • Data entry creates an index so the record can be found by name.
  • The document is optically scanned and microfilmed to meet state archival requirements.
  • The original returns to the address typed on it.

Form rules appear in A.R.S. 11-480: a caption, an original, original signatures, a page no larger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches in type of ten point or larger, and a two inch top margin on page one.

sections.h2: Does Pinal County have a transfer tax, and what is the affidavit of property value?
sections.html:
The Recorder's fee schedule lists no charge based on the sale price, and the county explains the affidavit this way: A.R.S. 11-1133 and 11-1137(B) require buyers and sellers, or their agents, to complete and attest to an Affidavit of Real Property Value, and failing to do so is a class 2 misdemeanor. County assessors and the Department of Revenue use the data to build tables for uniform valuation. The county adds that data from one sale does not directly change the assessment or taxes on that property.

The affidavit is signed, notarized and submitted to the Recorder. Exempt transfers skip it. Under A.R.S. 11-1134, a deed of gift, a quitclaim deed for no monetary consideration, a trustee's deed, a transfer between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild or siblings for only nominal consideration, and a transfer under a beneficiary deed with only nominal consideration are all on the list.

If your transfer is exempt, the county instructs you to write the statute number and exemption code on the face of the deed beneath the legal description. Its example is "A.R.S. 11-1134 B3." Do not complete the affidavit in that case.

sections.h2: What if you need to fix or remove something on a recorded record?
sections.html:
The only way to change the public record is another recording. The county explains that once an instrument of transfer has been recorded, a later recorded document is how ownership changes. The Recorder cannot advise on how to hold title or how to remove a decedent's name from a deed, so those questions go to a title company or an attorney.

Two other points from the county's FAQ are useful to a seller.

  • To see easements on your property, check Schedule B of your title policy if the purchase closed through a title company. Otherwise search the Recorder's website using one party's name and an approximate recording date.
  • People who want personal information removed from public records should read the separate Arizona statutes for the Recorder (A.R.S. 11-483), the Assessor and Treasurer (A.R.S. 11-484) and voter registration (A.R.S. 16-153).

The office also warns that it may refer suspicious documents to the FBI or other law enforcement, and that presenting a false instrument for recording is a class 6 felony under A.R.S. 39-161.

sections.h2: What is Pinal County like for sellers?
sections.html:
Pinal County was carved out of Maricopa and Pima counties on February 1, 1875, and Florence is the seat. It covers 5,374 square miles and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate counts 539,380 residents, up from 425,264 in 2020. Wikipedia lists five cities (Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Coolidge, Eloy and Maricopa) and towns including Florence, Kearny, Superior and San Tan Valley, which is the largest community.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show 81.7 percent owner-occupied housing, a median owner-occupied value of $349,000, median gross rent of $1,537 and median household income of $80,266. The county has 161,917 households. Sellers in Maricopa or San Tan Valley can use the nearby Recorder offices listed above instead of driving to Florence.

faqs.q: How much does Pinal County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: $30 per document, or $15 for recordings requested by government bodies. The fee includes the affidavit of property value, indexing and the storage surcharge, plus $1 for mailing the document back. Plats and survey maps run $24 for the first sheet.

faqs.q: Where is the Pinal County Recorder's main office?
faqs.a: 31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence, AZ 85132. Branch offices operate in Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley. All are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed in Pinal County by mail or online?
faqs.a: Yes. You can mail the original with a check or money order, or record electronically through a trusted e-recording partner. Contact a Pinal County Recorder's office for the partner list. Mail requests need the amount from the current fee schedule.

faqs.q: Do I need to file an affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: Yes, unless your transfer is exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134. Buyers and sellers must complete and attest to it, and failing to do so is a class 2 misdemeanor. For an exempt transfer, write the statute and exemption code on the face of the deed instead.

faqs.q: Can the Pinal County Recorder prepare my deed or notarize it?
faqs.a: No. The Recorder does not provide notary services and is prohibited from giving legal advice, assisting with documents or suggesting which documents to use. Have an attorney, title company or escrow officer prepare the deed and arrange the notary.
